expectedText:
LIFE ESTATE DEED — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Morgan

PURPOSE OF THIS LIFE ESTATE DEED INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes a deed reserving a life estate — a form of property conveyance recognized under California's Civil Code by which an owner of real property conveys a remainder interest in that property to another person now, while the transferor keeps the exclusive right to possess and use the property for the rest of the transferor's life. It is a different instrument from a revocable transfer-on-death deed and from a living trust, both of which this corpus describes in separate documents. This Information Sheet concerns a deed by Pat Morgan, reserving a life estate, conveying a remainder interest in the real property located at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, described as Lot 12, Block 3, Tract No. 4567, as per map recorded in Book 45, Page 12 of Maps, Sacramento County Records, to Jordan Morgan. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing California statutes and reported case law about life estates; it is not a deed, a legal opinion, or advice about whether reserving a life estate is an appropriate way to convey any specific property, or about the tax, Medi-Cal, or other consequences for Pat Morgan or Jordan Morgan of doing so.

LIFE ESTATES AS A RECOGNIZED CATEGORY OF REAL PROPERTY ESTATE
California's Civil Code classifies every estate in real property, by the duration of its enjoyment, into one of four categories. A life estate — an estate lasting for the duration of someone's life — is one of those four listed categories, distinct from an estate of inheritance (a fee simple, which lasts perpetually), an estate for years (a lease), or an estate at will.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Estates in real property, in respect to the duration of their enjoyment are either: l. Estates of inheritance or perpetual estates; 2. Estates for life; 3. Estates for years; or, 4. Estates at will."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 761, California Civil Code, the four durational categories of estates in real property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=761.)
  Known gap: The statutory text itself contains a formatting oddity that this clause preserves rather than silently corrects: the first item in the list is numbered with a lowercase letter “l.” rather than the numeral “1.” in the version currently published by the California Legislative Information website (verified directly against the raw fetched HTML, which renders the same character both times the section was fetched). This clause lists the four categories the statute names; it does not itself state what rights or duties attach to a life estate specifically (addressed in other clauses of this document), and it does not address how a life estate is created by a particular deed.

A LIFE ESTATE'S CLASSIFICATION AS A FREEHOLD ESTATE
California law places a life estate in the same broader classification as a fee simple estate: both are “estates of freehold,” a classification distinct from a lease (a “chattel real”) or a tenancy at will (a “chattel interest”).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Estates of inheritance and for life are called estates of freehold; estates for years are chattels real; and estates at will are chattel interests, but are not subject to enforcement of a money judgment."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 765, California Civil Code, freehold classification of estates of inheritance and for life (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=765.)
  Known gap: This clause is definitional and classificatory only. It does not itself state what rights, duties, or remedies attach to a freehold estate beyond this durational classification — those are addressed, for a life estate specifically, in other clauses of this document — and it does not address recording, tax, or Medi-Cal consequences of holding or creating a freehold estate.

WHY A DEED MUST EXPRESSLY RESERVE A LIFE ESTATE
A deed's default legal effect in California is to convey the fee simple — full ownership — of the property it describes. California law presumes that a fee simple title is intended to pass by any grant of real property, unless the grant itself shows that a lesser estate, such as a life estate, was intended. A deed meant to reserve a life estate to the grantor while conveying only a remainder interest to the grantee must therefore say so on its face.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "A fee simple title is presumed to be intended to pass by a grant of real property, unless it appears from the grant that a lesser estate was intended."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1105, California Civil Code, fee-simple title presumed from a grant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1105.)
  Known gap: This presumption in § 1105 applies to any grant of real property, not only to one attempting to reserve a life estate; this clause does not evaluate whether the wording of any particular deed — including the deed described in this document — achieves an effective reservation of a life estate, and it does not address other formalities a deed also requires, such as execution, acknowledgment, or recording, which this corpus addresses in its Grant Deed document.

THE LIFE TENANT'S STATUTORY DUTY TO MAINTAIN THE PROPERTY AND PAY TAXES
While a life estate is in effect, California law places two ongoing statutory obligations on the life tenant: to keep the buildings and fences on the property in repair from ordinary wear (which the statute calls “ordinary waste”), and to pay the property taxes and other annual charges, along with a just proportion of any extraordinary assessment that benefits the whole inheritance.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The owner of a life estate must keep the buildings and fences in repair from ordinary waste, and must pay the taxes and other annual charges, and a just proportion of extraordinary assessments benefiting the whole inheritance."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 840, California Civil Code, life tenant's duty to repair and pay taxes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=840.)
  Known gap: This clause describes only the two obligations stated in this particular section. Section 840 does not itself specify who, as between the life tenant and the remainderman, bears the cost of extraordinary repairs, capital improvements, or insurance, and it does not itself state what remedy is available to a remainderman if a life tenant fails to meet these duties; this document does not address those separate questions.

THE LIFE TENANT'S USE OF THE PROPERTY, AND THE LIMIT AGAINST INJURING THE INHERITANCE
California law gives a life tenant broad freedom to use the property in the same manner an owner of a fee simple could, subject to one express statutory limit: the life tenant must do no act to the injury of “the inheritance” — the remainder interest that will pass to the remainderman when the life estate ends. Applying this section, a California Court of Appeal has held that whether a particular act amounts to such an injury turns on whether it results in a substantial depreciation of the property's market value, and that the burden of proving that depreciation rests on the remainderman bringing the claim.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The owner of a life estate may use the land in the same manner as the owner of a fee simple, except that he must do no act to the injury of the inheritance."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 818, California Civil Code, life tenant's use of the property and the limit against injury to the inheritance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=818.)
  "The burden of proving depreciation in market value of the land, as a result of the alleged wrongful acts of waste rests upon the remainderman, who must establish that fact by satisfactory evidence, even though a life tenant may not use what might appear to be the best of care in the cultivation and care of the property."
  — Sallee v. Daneri, 49 Cal. App. 2d 324, 121 P.2d 781 (Cal. Ct. App. 1942) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1317251/sallee-v-daneri/)
  Known gap: Sallee v. Daneri is a single intermediate appellate decision (Third Appellate District, decided January 1942); the California Supreme Court denied a petition for hearing, which leaves this Court of Appeal decision, not a Supreme Court opinion, as the controlling authority quoted here. The case itself involved a dispute over cutting timber and deteriorated farm buildings on agricultural land; this clause does not claim the same market-value-depreciation test would be applied identically to every other kind of act on every kind of property, and § 818 itself does not define “inheritance” or “injury.” This clause does not evaluate whether any specific act by any specific life tenant would constitute an injury to the inheritance.

HOW A DEED RESERVING A LIFE ESTATE DIFFERS FROM A REVOCABLE TRANSFER-ON-DEATH DEED
This corpus describes California's revocable transfer-on-death deed in a separate document. A deed reserving a life estate is a different kind of instrument: once it is executed and delivered, it is a present conveyance that immediately vests a remainder interest in the named remainderman — here, Jordan Morgan — rather than a transfer that takes effect only at the transferor's death and that the transferor may revoke unilaterally at any time before then, as a revocable transfer-on-death deed does. Changing or undoing a deed reserving a life estate after it has been delivered and accepted generally calls for a new conveyance signed by whoever then holds the remainder interest, rather than a unilateral act by the life tenant alone.

PROPERTY TAX CHANGE-IN-OWNERSHIP TREATMENT OF CREATING AND ENDING A LIFE ESTATE
For purposes of California's property tax reassessment rules, creating a life estate is treated differently from ending one. A transfer made by an instrument whose terms reserve to the transferor an estate for life is, by that reservation alone, excluded from the definition of a “change in ownership” that would otherwise trigger reassessment. California law separately provides that when that life estate later terminates, the termination itself does constitute a change in ownership, subject to certain other statutory exceptions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "(e) Any transfer by an instrument whose terms reserve to the transferor an estate for years or an estate for life. However, the termination of such an estate for years or estate for life shall constitute a change in ownership, except as provided in subdivision (d) and in Section 63."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 62(e), California Revenue and Taxation Code, change-in-ownership treatment of an instrument reserving an estate for life (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=62.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (e) of Revenue and Taxation Code § 62, a section with many other subdivisions addressing other kinds of transfers not described here. Subdivision (e) itself cross-references subdivision (d) and Section 63 as containing further exceptions to the termination-is-a-change-in-ownership rule; this clause does not quote or describe the content of subdivision (d) or Section 63, and it does not determine the reassessed value or resulting tax consequence for any specific property.

RECORDING AN AFFIDAVIT OF DEATH TO REFLECT THE END OF A LIFE ESTATE
When a life tenant dies, the remainder interest that a deed reserving a life estate already vested in the remainderman does not pass through probate. California law provides a mechanism to place the fact of that death on the public record for the property: any person may record, in the county where the property is located, an affidavit of death — executed by a person with knowledge of the facts, including a particular description of the real property and an attested or certified copy of the death record — establishing that title to the property was affected by a death.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "If title to real property is affected by the death of a person, any person may record in the county in which the property is located any of the following documents establishing the fact of the death: (a) An affidavit of death executed by a person having knowledge of the facts."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 210(a), California Probate Code, recording an affidavit of death to establish that title to real property was affected by a death (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=210.)
  Known gap: Probate Code § 210 applies broadly to any situation in which title to real property is affected by a death — it is the same statutory mechanism used, for example, to record an affidavit of death of a joint tenant — and is not written specifically for a life estate; no separate Probate Code section addresses life estates alone. This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of § 210; subdivision (b), not quoted here, separately allows recording a certified copy of a court order determining the fact of death under Probate Code Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 200) or another statute. Recording an affidavit of death under this section does not itself resolve any dispute about the validity of the original deed reserving the life estate or about who holds the remainder interest.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — LIFE ESTATE DEED INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet was prepared concerning a deed by Pat Morgan, reserving a life estate, conveying a remainder interest in the real property located at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, described as Lot 12, Block 3, Tract No. 4567, as per map recorded in Book 45, Page 12 of Maps, Sacramento County Records, in Sacramento County, to Jordan Morgan, and was executed on September 1, 2026 at Sacramento, California.
